subject: Critical Thinking
title: Noam Chomsky: Manufacturing Consent and Media Criticism
description: A micro-lesson that makes Noam Chomsky: Manufacturing Consent and Media Criticism usable.

hook.text: The media doesn't tell you what to think. It tells you what to THINK ABOUT.

discovery.text: Chomsky compared what media emphasized, omitted, and repeated to reveal hidden filters.

twist.text: The media isn't a conspiracy – it's a system.

climax.text: His tool for critical thinking: always compare how similar events are covered when the actors change.

punchline.text: Free press doesn't mean unbiased press. The filters are invisible.

quiz.question: What is Chomsky's 'propaganda model' of media?
options: Media is controlled by one person
Structural filters (ownership, advertising, sourcing) systematically shape news coverage

details.summary: Noam Chomsky's propaganda model argues that mass media systematically filters information to serve elite interests rather than informing the public. Ownership, advertising, sourcing, and ideological conformity create predictable biases.
details.whyItMatters: Chomsky's analysis provides a framework for understanding why media coverage is systematically biased in predictable directions, essential for media literacy.
takeaways: Media serves elite interests through structural filters, not conspiracies
Five filters shape news: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, and ideology
Manufacturing Consent became a foundational text in media criticism

faq.question: What are the five filters of the propaganda model?
faq.answer: Ownership (media concentration), advertising (revenue dependence), sourcing (reliance on official sources), flak (negative responses to unfavorable reporting), and ideological filters. These structural pressures shape coverage without any explicit conspiracy.

faq.question: Is Chomsky's propaganda model still relevant in the age of social media?
faq.answer: The structural filters have evolved but persist. Social media platforms are owned by powerful corporations, driven by advertising revenue, subject to government pressure, and use algorithms that can amplify rather than counteract propaganda.
